title: PHP October 2026: the briefing
subtitle: Two critical PHP flaws (php2shell): what it is, where it stands, what we know, and the bottom line
for: anyone who has to present the situation: to a board, a team, a client or a class
rule: Dated and kept as made: every number on a slide names the file it comes from and the gate checks it while the deck is current; every slide cites the evidence vault's source slugs; status words are the site's (confirmed, reported, disputed, contradicted, unverified). Where a slide uses evidence newer than 11:34 UTC it says so on the slide.

slides.title: PHP October 2026
slides.lead: Two critical security flaws in PHP, the software behind many of the world's websites. The briefing, dated.
slides.dateline: Thursday 22 October 2026 · evidence as of 11:34 UTC · vault commit 200d08971937 · site v0.5.2
slides.note: Say the date and time first. Everything on these slides is as of 11:34 UTC on 22 October, the latest page the evidence vault saved; the site and the slides will move when the evidence does.

slides.title: The bottom line

points.head: Fix it
points.text: Update PHP to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, and restart it. Installed is not running.

points.head: No panic, no complacency
points.text: Attackers are trying in large numbers; no organisation has confirmed a break-in.

points.head: Decide offline now
points.text: If a system cannot be patched today, name who can take it offline, and when. The agencies disagree, so the decision is yours.

slides.note: The answer first. If the room remembers one slide, it is this one: update and restart; trying is not breaking in; own the offline decision before you need it.

slides.title: What it is

points.text: Someone anywhere on the internet, with no password, can use them against a website that has not installed the fix, and make its server run their own commands.
Proven on Apache mod_php with default settings; on PHP-FPM it is disputed.
Not your phone or laptop: the flaw is on web servers.

slides.note: Press calls the pair php2shell. Two separate bugs, one advisory. The traditional Apache setup is the proven case; other setups are likely but less certain.

slides.title: How it unfolded

moments.what: An audit spots the out-of-memory weakness. Nobody can show it is exploitable, so it is left.
Three teams using AI turn it into working attacks within three weeks and report them to PHP.
The secret leaks: the CVE numbers circulate two days early, with a wrong severity score.
PHP releases the fix a day ahead of plan. Firewall vendors already have rules live.
Agencies warn: update, or take systems offline. Sites go dark as a precaution.

slides.note: Two things to stress: AI-assisted research turned an old audit finding into working attacks; and the leak moved the release a day early, so defenders and attackers started the clock together.

slides.title: Where it stands now

stats.label: on CISA's exploited list
stats.sub: neither flaw, at the latest check

points.text: Some organisations took websites offline as a precaution, among them Dutch government services such as the DigiD login.
Offline is a decision, not evidence of a hack.

slides.note: Attempts are requests, not sites, and not compromises. The ten organisations offline come mostly from one news live page and are not all confirmed by the organisations named.

slides.title: How sure we are
slides.lead: 70 statements checked. Confirmed means two or more original sources agree.

points.text: The headline '70% of the Internet' is not what it sounds like. It is roughly the share of websites built with PHP, which is what the same company's own article says; nobody has measured how many are actually at risk.
Each statement, its status and its saved sources: php.oct.2026.newsroom.sgit.ai/claims/

slides.note: This is the slide for a journalist or a sceptic. Most of what circulates is reported by one party; say which.

slides.title: Exposed is not exploited

steps.label: hit, and holding something worth reaching

slides.note: Each rung is a different count by a different party. The number that matters, the last one, nobody has measured: what a compromised server could reach.

slides.title: What governments say
slides.lead: Every agency: install the fix. If you cannot, they disagree.

points.text: US (NSA, CISA): take it offline. UK (NCSC): consider it, after the temporary mitigations. EU, France, Canada: isolate from public networks.

slides.note: Two agencies could not be read (bot challenges) and are counted as not read, not as silent.

slides.title: Who gets a fix

cols.head: Supported: fixed
points: OS packages from 15:30 UTC (Red Hat first)

cols.head: End of life: partial
points: 7.4: a mitigation commit on a branch

cols.head: Products built on PHP
points: 724 in the Dutch NCSC list at 15:28 UTC

slides.later: The product counts are from the NCSC-NL list at 15:28 UTC, after the 11:34 capture.
slides.note: The long tail is the story of the next weeks: products that bundle PHP, and servers on versions PHP no longer supports.

slides.title: What nobody knows yet

points.text: Whether any website was actually broken into before it installed the fix.
Whether the fix is complete. A report on 21 October suggested it may not be; the PHP project has not answered it publicly yet.
Who leaked the news on 20 October, and where.
Exactly which websites went offline, and why. Most of the list comes from one news live page and has not been confirmed by the organisations named.
Where the 70% figure comes from. None of the pages that use it says how it was measured.

slides.note: Stated, not papered over. These are the questions to watch; the site updates each one when the evidence does.

slides.title: What to do, by who you are

cols.head: You run a website
points: Ask your host which PHP version is serving your site now, and when it was restarted
Ask whether anything still runs PHP 8.1 or older

cols.head: You run the servers
points: Patch and restart every PHP process
No patch today: the temporary settings, an edge rule, then offline

cols.head: You own the risk
points: Name who can take a system offline
Ask for evidence you were not hit
